props.title: The Ten Commandments
props.initialSlug: Epic tale of Moses leading Hebrews to freedom

sections.content: Cecil B. DeMille's silent epic The Ten Commandments revolutionized biblical spectacle filmmaking, setting the template that Hollywood would follow for decades. Its massive sets, including a 120-foot-tall Egyptian city gate and life-sized sphinx, established new standards for production design. While less known than DeMille's 1956 remake with Charlton Heston, this original version pioneered many visual effects techniques, particularly in its parting of the Red Sea sequence achieved through gelatin and a split-screen effect. The film actually tells two stories - the biblical Exodus narrative and a modern morality tale about two brothers, demonstrating how DeMille connected ancient religious themes to contemporary social issues.

sections.content: The success of The Ten Commandments sparked a wave of biblical epics in the silent era. King of Kings (1927), also directed by DeMille, brought unprecedented scale to depicting the life of Jesus. These films established a visual language for biblical storytelling: massive sets, thousands of extras, and innovative effects work. The genre's popularity demonstrated early Hollywood's ability to merge spectacle with moral messaging, something that would become crucial to the industry's self-regulation under the later Production Code. SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Visual Effects

Silent-era biblical epics pushed technical boundaries out of necessity. The Ten Commandments used groundbreaking practical effects, while Ben-Hur (1925) employed early Technicolor sequences. These innovations carried forward into films like Noah's Ark (1928), though that production's dangerous flood sequence, which injured many extras, led to stricter safety regulations. DeMille's work particularly influenced Sign of the Cross (1932), showing how silent techniques evolved into the sound era.
